source.title: Multimodal indicators of non-functional overreaching in NCAA Division I American football athletes: evidence for role-specific physiological adaptation

paper.citation: Aychman M.M., Vinson K., Tasnim N., Perez J., Hodes G.E., Basso J.C. Multimodal indicators of non-functional overreaching in NCAA Division I American football athletes: evidence for role-specific physiological adaptation. Frontiers in Physiology. 2026;17:1818629. doi:10.3389/fphys.2026.1818629.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How do salivary biomarkers, countermovement-jump measures, workload, sleep, and soreness change across a season, and do associations differ by team role? Thirty-nine male NCAA Division I football athletes, ages 18–25. One program across a 15-week competitive season. Longitudinal observational monitoring. Pre-, mid-, and postseason saliva assessed cortisol, testosterone, IL-6, and TNF-α.
paper.tldr: Among starters, higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratios were associated with lower soreness and better sleep; IL-6/cortisol was associated with RSImod. Nonstarters showed different associations, including poorer recovery alongside higher IL-6/cortisol despite lower external load. Separate starter and developmental-player exposure histories when reviewing fatigue signals.
paper.methods: Longitudinal observational monitoring. Pre-, mid-, and postseason saliva assessed cortisol, testosterone, IL-6, and TNF-α. CMJ, PlayerLoad, sleep quality, and soreness were tracked and analyzed through associations.
paper.findings: Among starters, higher testosterone-to-cortisol ratios were associated with lower soreness and better sleep; IL-6/cortisol was associated with RSImod. Nonstarters showed different associations, including poorer recovery alongside higher IL-6/cortisol despite lower external load. The authors interpreted IL-6/cortisol as a potentially informative multimodal signal, not a standalone diagnosis. Role-specific patterns were exploratory and did not establish that measured athletes had clinically confirmed NFOR.
paper.limitations: Small convenience sample from one team and one season. Subgroup models may be underpowered and overfit. Associations cannot establish causal pathways or individual diagnostic cutoffs. Biomarker timing and analytic reliability matter before applied use.
paper.practicalImplications: Separate starter and developmental-player exposure histories when reviewing fatigue signals. Use biomarkers only alongside workload, CMJ strategy, sleep, soreness, illness, and performance—never as a single clearance or NFOR threshold.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, separate starter and developmental-player exposure histories when reviewing fatigue signals. Use biomarkers only alongside workload, CMJ strategy, sleep, soreness, illness, and performance—never as a single clearance or NFOR threshold. Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
